solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Thinking credulously that someone likes you?

definitions.text: Thinking credulously that someone likes you?

blocks.note: surface reading: naively trusting in something
setter's reading: a conviction that another person is fond of you

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means a cherished but naive conviction; the clue reads 'fond' as 'liking', so it becomes believing someone is fond of you.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherished, rather naive conviction is called by this phrase, and wishful thinking about being liked is exactly such a credulous notion.

clue.text: Regarding as past history

blocks.note: first meaning: concerning, as in 'a row about money'
second meaning: finished and done with

explanation.surface: Someone treats an old matter as belonging to the past.
explanation.definitionFit: The preposition means concerning (a quarrel ___ money), and the adjective means finished or ended, like a thing consigned to history.

clue.text: Keep for a fellow-man

blocks.note: a don is a fellow of a university college
a man's name

explanation.surface: Someone saves a thing for a fellow human being.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: the strongest tower of a castle. The hyphen in 'fellow-man' joins two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A donjon is the great central tower of a medieval castle, which is what the word keep also names.

clue.text: With the backing of number one, might authorise

indicators.note: backing suggests going backwards, so the word for number one is read from its end

blocks.note: number one is oneself
might means strength

explanation.surface: Supported by the boss, a person could perhaps give permission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might' looks like a verb meaning 'could', but it is the noun meaning strength.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone official authority or legal permission to act is to grant them that capacity, a close synonym of authorise.

clue.text: It's hard to smooth things over

blocks.note: first meaning: a hard metal
second meaning: press creases out of clothes

explanation.surface: Someone laments how difficult it is to calm down a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth things over' suggests making peace; here it is literal pressing of laundry.
explanation.definitionFit: The metal is proverbially tough, and the household appliance of the same name presses fabric flat, the verb meaning remove wrinkles.

clue.text: He got caught entering – a daft stupid fool!

indicators.note: a stupid arrangement is a muddled one, so the preceding words are jumbled
something caught entering ends up trapped inside the other piece

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man barged in, and the speaker calls him a foolish idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface piles up insults, so 'daft' and 'stupid' look like part of the definition; only 'fool' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: This colloquial insult for a dim-witted person is a common equivalent of fool or idiot.

clue.text: As the donor said, on finding one after a search?

definitions.text: As the donor said, on finding one after a search?

blocks.note: surface reading: words spoken when handing over a gift

blocks.clueFragment: on finding one after a search
blocks.note: setter's reading: what someone exclaims on locating the thing looked for

explanation.walkthrough: The same everyday phrase serves both when presenting something to someone and when announcing that a missing item has turned up.
explanation.definitionFit: This expression is said both when handing over a gift and when producing a sought item, so both situations in the clue fit.

clue.text: Within a short time cheat, being fickle

indicators.note: within places one item inside the other, so the cheat goes in the middle of the short time

blocks.note: a moment
to swindle

explanation.surface: Someone is unfaithful quickly, showing how changeable they are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cheat' looks like the act of an unfaithful lover in the surface, but it is just a swindle, and the short time is split open to take it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone changeable in loyalty or affection is not steady, which is the meaning of both words.

clue.text: Able to cut to achieve prices that are competitive

blocks.note: first meaning: sharp, of a blade
second meaning: low, of prices offered to beat rivals

explanation.surface: A shop is in a position to slash costs so as to match rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Able to cut' suggests cutting prices; it describes a sharp edge.
explanation.definitionFit: A blade with a fine edge is sharp, and prices pitched low to beat rivals are described with the same adjective in British retail.

clue.text: Only a person working in a Chinese restaurant can provide it

definitions.text: Only a person working in a Chinese restaurant can provide it

blocks.clueFragment: Only a person working in a Chinese restaurant
blocks.note: surface reading: a specialist dish only the restaurant's staff can supply
setter's reading: a common stir-fry ingredient served in such restaurants

explanation.walkthrough: A loose cryptic definition: the item is a staple vegetable of Chinese cooking, so the restaurant's kitchen is where it comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: The crisp shoot of a germinated mung bean is a familiar ingredient in Chinese stir-fries and chop suey.

clue.text: Stopped at an English resort for the purpose of

blocks.note: Hove is a seaside town next to Brighton in Sussex
as in 'came to help'

explanation.surface: Someone halted at a seaside town in England for some reason.
explanation.walkthrough: Hove is a seaside town on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailing ship that has turned into the wind and come to a halt is said in nautical language to have done this.

clue.text: Many marked for identification purposes were frightened

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword stand-in for many
as birds are tagged with leg rings

explanation.surface: A crowd who were tagged so they could be identified felt afraid.
explanation.walkthrough: Many = C is the convention of C as a hundred. Birds are ringed so they can be identified later.
explanation.definitionFit: To shrink back or recoil in fear is to have been frightened, so the past-tense verb matches the plural phrase.

clue.text: Lay in bed

blocks.note: surface reading: past tense of lie, someone stayed between the sheets
setter's reading: a lay is a song, here one sung over a baby's cot

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay' looks like the past tense of lie; it is the old noun for a song, and the bed is a baby's.
explanation.definitionFit: A lullaby sung to soothe an infant to sleep beside its cot is a song for a baby's bed.

clue.text: Where a child finds fingers useful as well

definitions.text: Where a child finds fingers useful

blocks.clueFragment: Where a child finds fingers useful
blocks.note: first meaning: doing sums, when a youngster counts on fingers
second meaning: also, besides

explanation.surface: A small child counts on fingers, and they are handy for other things too.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means also or besides, and read literally it places a child doing sums, where counting on fingers helps.

clue.text: Takes out and one eats them

blocks.note: first meaning: goes out romantically with
second meaning: sweet fruit of a palm

explanation.surface: Someone extracts something and then eats it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes out' suggests removing; it means escorting someone on romantic outings.
explanation.definitionFit: To court someone with outings is a verb sense, and the sticky palm fruit is eaten fresh or dried.

clue.text: Agents and fellow members of the cast

blocks.note: F is a standard abbreviation for fellow
the people in a play's cast

explanation.surface: Talent agents and other performers in the same production.
explanation.definitionFit: A factor is a person who buys or sells goods on commission for someone else, a business representative.

clue.text: Tired and hungry? No

blocks.note: first meaning: weary and bored of something
second meaning, read literally: having eaten one's fill

explanation.surface: Someone is weary and peckish, then corrects themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means sick of something; taken literally it means well fed, hence not hungry.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means weary of something, and read word by word it says one has been fed, the opposite of hungry.

clue.text: The wagtail, my love, was upset about – was cross

indicators.note: the bird's name splits in two, and its second half, tail, says keep only the end of the first half
something upset is overturned, so the term of endearment reads the other way
about means around, so the turned term of endearment surrounds the kept letter

blocks.note: a term of endearment
the end of this word

explanation.surface: Someone's darling was distressed over a small bird and became angry.
explanation.walkthrough: The wagtail is a bird, but here the word splits into wag + tail. The first 'was' belongs to the reversal phrase; the second starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To have been in a fury or angry outburst is to have been cross, matching tense and part of speech.

clue.text: That, son, is a fruit – and fruit was his undoing

indicators.note: the answer with the young male added makes the fruit, so taking that word away leaves the answer

blocks.note: an indefinite article followed by a small plum
taken as written

explanation.surface: A father points out a fruit to his boy, then recalls a man ruined by fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That' is the answer itself: the answer plus SON spells A DAMSON. The first man was expelled from Eden after eating the forbidden fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the first man was expelled from Eden for eating the forbidden fruit, so fruit brought about his downfall.

clue.text: Shut up with a loony

blocks.note: to silence
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is told to be quiet while sitting beside a madman.
explanation.definitionFit: This informal word for someone mentally confused or crazy is a slang equivalent of loony.

clue.text: Come out on the date – first and last sections only

indicators.note: the first and last sections of a word are its opening and closing letters

blocks.note: its two end letters
as in 'but a child'

explanation.surface: Someone appears on the appointed day, with only the start and finish shown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only' looks like part of the instruction, but it gives BUT.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a first public appearance, as a debutante does, is to come out; the word also works as a verb.

clue.text: Medicine administered, comes round

blocks.note: liquid medicine taken in drops
put in, taken in

explanation.surface: A patient given a drug regains consciousness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes round' suggests waking up; it means paying a casual visit.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay an informal visit without arranging it first is to call by, which is what comes round means.

clue.text: Witless twit the composer's going on tours with

definitions.note: read as a noun: one's journeys

indicators.note: witless means lacking wit, so those three letters are removed from the next word

blocks.note: taken as written
Maurice Ravel, French composer of Boléro

explanation.surface: A foolish idiot is accompanying a composer on concert tours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Witless' looks like an insult describing the twit; it tells you to drop WIT from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's journeys abroad, the act of going on tours, are collectively called by this plural noun.

clue.text: Runs going down the steps

blocks.note: first meaning: snags running down tights or stockings
second meaning: frames of rungs for climbing

explanation.surface: Someone hurries down a staircase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' suggests moving fast; in British usage a run in tights is called by the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A vertical tear in stockings is known by this word in Britain, and a stepladder or rung frame is also called this.

clue.text: Current, or power, enters when switched on

indicators.note: switched suggests letters being swapped around into another order

blocks.note: P is the physics symbol for power
taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: An electricity statement: current or power flows when a switch is turned on.
explanation.walkthrough: The electrical surface makes 'Current' look like electricity; it means existing now.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening now, of the existing moment, is described as current, an adjective synonym.

clue.text: She doesn't allow the dances to start up

indicators.note: not allowing something means leaving it out, here the opening letter
names which letter is refused: the one at the very beginning of the word
in a down light reading up means from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: theatrical dance performances

explanation.surface: A woman refuses to let the dancing begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to start' points at the first letter of the dances, which is removed before the rest is read upward.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a woman's first name, and a female person can be referred to in crossword clues simply as she.

clue.text: Shows sudden interest in the thing the cat's carrying back

indicators.note: back means the pet's name is read from its last letter to its first
carrying means holding within, so the cat surrounds the thing

blocks.note: an affectionate name for a cat
a pronoun for any thing

explanation.surface: Someone perks up at whatever the cat is bringing home.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in 'cat's' stands for 'is' in the surface; the wordplay only needs the cat.
explanation.definitionFit: To straighten in one's seat and become alert is the idiom for suddenly paying attention.

clue.text: It's not only caught by the elderly!

definitions.text: It's not only caught by the elderly!

blocks.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
old people

explanation.surface: An illness people of every age pick up, not just pensioners.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: a common infection caught by people of all ages.
explanation.definitionFit: The common viral infection of the nose and throat is something anyone catches, young or old.

clue.text: Ann, if dumped by the financier, can resort to him

indicators.note: letters dumped by a word are thrown out of it
to re-sort is to sort again into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letters to be thrown out

explanation.surface: A woman jilted by a money man can turn to another man for comfort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort to' looks like turning to someone; 'resort' is read as re-sort.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a man's first name, so a male person may stand for it, referred to by the pronoun him.

clue.text: Advertisement about cigarettes being bad for you?

definitions.text: Advertisement about cigarettes being bad for you?

blocks.clueFragment: Advertisement about cigarettes being bad for you
blocks.note: surface reading: an anti-smoking health campaign
setter's reading: a device that announces, with a loud noise, that fumes are present

explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like a health warning poster; it is a device that warns of fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A household detector that sounds a loud warning when it senses fumes is a notice that burning is dangerous.

clue.text: The green light just after, on turning the corner

indicators.note: turning round means the short word is read from its end

blocks.note: taken as written
approval, the go-ahead

explanation.surface: A driver gets the go signal just after rounding a bend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just after' places the go-ahead after the turned word.
explanation.definitionFit: A small secluded recess or angle of a room is a synonym of corner, as in every nook and cranny.

clue.text: Agree when I take the attitude it's close

definitions.note: the phrase means a short way off

blocks.note: assent with a head movement
taken as written
to adopt a position or point of view

explanation.surface: Someone agrees when they adopt a position that the result is tight.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying a place is only a short way away, very near at hand, means it is nearby.
